problemText: Starting from Earth's surface and moving straight down toward the center, what is the correct order of Earth's three layers?
choices: Crust, mantle, core
Mantle, crust, core
Core, mantle, crust
Crust, core, mantle
hints: The crust is the outermost layer, closest to the surface where you stand.
Each layer sits closer to Earth's center than the one before it.

problemText: A geologist finds solid rock material during a drilling project. She knows she is still in Earth's outermost layer, and she also knows that no one has ever drilled deeper than this layer in most places on Earth. Which layer is she drilling through?
choices: The mantle, because it is made of solid rock and people have drilled deep enough to reach it in many locations around the world
The crust, because it is solid rock and is the only layer people have actually reached by drilling
The core, because it is the deepest layer people try to drill toward and contains solid rock material
The mantle, because it fills more of Earth's inside than the crust does and lies just below the surface
hints: The lesson explains which layer people have been able to actually drill into directly.
Think about which layer sits right under the ground and the ocean floor.

problemText: A scientist describes a layer of Earth as extremely hot and made of solid rock, and explains that it sits between two other layers. Based on the lesson, which layer is being described?
choices: The crust, which is solid rock and sits between the mantle and the core
The core, which is made of metal and sits at the very center of Earth
The mantle, which is solid rock and sits between the crust and the core
The crust, which is the hottest of the three layers and made entirely of solid rock
hints: Remember that the mantle is in the middle position, between two other layers.
The mantle is solid rock, but it is not the hottest layer — the core is.

problemText: A student compares two samples. Sample A is thin, solid rock, and is the only layer people have ever reached by drilling. Sample B is made mostly of metal and sits at Earth's very center, farther from the surface than any other point inside the planet. Which of the following correctly identifies both samples and explains why they are different layers?
choices: Sample A is the mantle and Sample B is the core; they are different because the mantle is solid rock while the core is metal
Sample A is the mantle and Sample B is the crust; the mantle is solid rock while the crust is made of metal
Sample A is the crust and Sample B is the mantle; they differ because the crust is thin while the mantle fills most of Earth's inside
Sample A is the crust and Sample B is the core; the crust is thin and reachable by drilling, while the core is metal and at the very center
hints: The crust is the only layer that people have actually drilled into directly.
The core is the layer at Earth's very center, and it is made of metal, not rock.

problemText: A geophysicist describes a layer by combining two kinds of clues: it fills more of Earth's inside space than the other two layers do, and it is solid rock. Based on the lesson, why is this description enough to identify the layer correctly, even though two layers are made of rock?
choices: Because the description rules out the core, which is metal, and the crust, which is thin; only the mantle fills most of Earth's inside and is solid rock
Because the crust is not actually made of solid rock but of loose material, so the rock clue immediately points to the mantle as the only solid rock layer
Because the core is made of rock and fills space inside Earth, making it the only layer that matches both descriptions given
Because size is the primary way to identify layers, and only the mantle is large enough to account for most of Earth's interior volume
hints: The core is made of metal, not rock, so it can be ruled out immediately.
Of the two rock layers, which one is thin and which one fills most of the space inside Earth?

problemText: A student reads that scientists know the mantle is extremely hot and made of solid rock, even though no one has ever drilled anywhere close to it. Explain why the lesson suggests that scientists could use a combination of clues — position and composition — to identify a layer correctly without reaching it, and describe which clues would rule out a layer being the crust instead of the mantle.
choices: Scientists can identify the mantle by its extreme heat and metal composition, which are opposite to the crust's cool temperature and rock makeup

A layer can be identified by where it sits or by what it is made of; the mantle sits in the middle between two other layers and is solid rock, unlike the crust which is solid rock but sits closest to the surface and is much thinner

The mantle must be extremely hot because it sits deeper inside Earth than the crust, and heat increases with depth in Earth's interior, so any layer that occupies the middle region must be hotter than the layer nearest the surface

Scientists identify the mantle by determining that the crust cannot extend all the way through Earth's interior, which means some other solid rock layer must occupy the space between the crust and the core
hints: Both the crust and mantle are solid rock, so composition alone does not separate them; you need position clues too.
Think about the thinness of the crust compared to how much space the mantle fills inside Earth.

problemText: What is a tectonic plate? Choose the best definition.
choices: A continent that is surrounded by water on all sides
One of the large slabs that Earth's rocky outer shell is broken into
A layer of melted rock underneath Earth's crust that plates float on
A single piece of ocean floor that does not move
hints: Remember that Earth's outer shell is not one unbroken piece.
The lesson uses the word 'slabs' to describe these rocky pieces.

problemText: A student measures that a tectonic plate moves 4 centimeters in one year. At this rate, how far will the plate move in 1,000 years?
choices: 4 centimeters total, because plates move at a constant speed that never changes
4 kilometers, which would definitely shift continents noticeably
40 meters, which is still too small to see on a world map
40 centimeters, which would push continents into new positions within a century
hints: Multiply the movement per year by the number of years.
Think about whether the result would be big enough to redraw a world map.

problemText: A student says that continents are boats floating on an underground ocean of melted rock. According to the lesson, what is wrong with this idea?
choices: Continents are not boats because they are made of solid rock instead of wood and cannot float on water like a boat does
Melted rock underground is called magma or lava, not an ocean, and the layer beneath plates is not actually liquid but extremely hot solid rock that moves very slowly
Continents move too slowly to be boats, and boats move on water while the rock below plates is solid material that creeps rather than flows like water does
The rock below the plates is solid, not liquid, even though it is extremely hot and can creep slowly over long time periods
hints: The lesson specifically corrects the idea that plates float on liquid.
Think about what the rock below the plates actually is, and how it can still move even if it is not liquid.

problemText: Geographers found that the same type of ancient rock forms a band along the west coast of Africa and another band along the east coast of South America, with the same age and the same pattern on both sides. When combined with the fact that these two coasts have matching shapes, what can geographers conclude? Explain why one piece of evidence alone would not be enough.
choices: The two coasts were once joined together, because matching rocks and matching shapes are two different kinds of evidence that both point to the same conclusion
The two coasts have never been joined because similar rocks can form in different places by coincidence, and coastline shapes alone are not enough proof of continental movement
The two coasts were briefly connected by a land bridge that later sank underwater, which would explain the rock patterns but not necessarily the matching coast shapes
The two coasts could be separate by chance because one type of evidence, whether rocks or shapes, is not strong enough on its own to prove continents were once connected
hints: One clue is a hunch, but three clues of different kinds are evidence.
Rock patterns are a completely different type of evidence from coastline shapes, so together they are stronger than one alone.

problemText: A scientist marks every earthquake and every volcano on a globe using data from the past year. Instead of spreading evenly across Earth's surface, the marks create a pattern. What does this pattern reveal about where tectonic plates are, and why?
choices: The marks show where continents are located, and they demonstrate that earthquakes and volcanoes occur primarily where land masses meet because plates only move where ground exists above them
The marks show where plate edges meet, because the middle of a plate is quiet but the rim is where plates push and grind against each other

The marks show where the hottest parts of Earth are located, since intense heat deep underground causes rocks to break and magma to rise, producing earthquakes and volcanoes wherever temperature reaches a certain level
The marks show the location of Pangaea, because ancient supercontinents experience more tectonic activity than modern continental arrangements do
hints: The lesson states that earthquakes and volcanoes crowd along long bands that trace the edges where one plate meets another.
Think about the difference between what happens at the edge of a plate and what happens in the middle of one.

problemText: A student reads that a tectonic plate moved 3 centimeters per year for the past 100 million years. She calculates the total distance and gets 3,000 kilometers. She then says: 'This proves that plates move fast, not slow, so the lesson must be wrong about the speed.' Identify the flaw in her reasoning and explain why the lesson's description of plate speed as very slow is still correct.
choices: Her reasoning is sound; the lesson should be updated to describe plate movement as fast rather than slow because the total distance traveled is very large
Her math contains an error because multiplying 3 centimeters per year by 100 million years should yield only 3 kilometers total, not 3,000 kilometers
Her math is correct, but 3,000 kilometers over 100 million years is still a very slow speed because the time period is enormous, and it took that entire span for the plates to move that far
Her conclusion is reasonable because continental drift clearly proves that plates travel thousands of kilometers in relatively short time periods, which would support her claim that movement is rapid
hints: The lesson emphasizes that plates move a few centimeters per year, which is about the speed fingernails grow—and asks you to think about whether that is fast or slow.
Consider whether something can move far if given enough time, yet still be described as moving very slowly.

problemText: Which of the following describes how igneous rock forms? Choose the statement that matches the definition taught in class.
choices: When an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting
When loose pieces of rock and sand are pressed together over time
When melted rock cools and hardens into a solid
When sediment settles in layers at the bottom of a river or ocean
hints: Think about what the word 'igneous' refers to — melted rock that has hardened.
The definition must include the word 'melt' or 'melted' to be correct.

problemText: A geologist finds a rock that is made of tiny grains of mud and sand that have been squeezed tightly together into solid rock. She knows these grains settled into a layer at the bottom of an ancient lake over millions of years. What type of rock is this, and why?
choices: Igneous rock, because the grains came from a water environment
Igneous rock, because the pressure from overlying layers eventually hardened it
Metamorphic rock, because the rock has been buried deep underground
Sedimentary rock, because loose pieces settled into a layer and were pressed together
hints: Look for the words that tell you how the rock formed — did loose pieces settle and get pressed together?
Metamorphic rock requires heat and pressure to change an *existing* rock, but this rock formed from loose pieces, not from an existing rock being squeezed.

problemText: A rock formed when magma erupted from a volcano and cooled quickly at Earth's surface into solid rock. Which rock type is this, and what rule or definition tells you so?
choices: Igneous rock, because melted rock cooled and hardened into a solid
Metamorphic rock, because intense heat was involved in the process
Sedimentary rock, because the cooling happened in layers
Metamorphic rock, because the rock changed form without melting completely
hints: The word 'magma' means melted rock — so melted rock cooled. Which rock type forms that way?
Even though the rock got very hot, the key process here is cooling and hardening of melted rock, not being changed by heat and pressure.

problemText: An existing metamorphic rock is heated so intensely underground that it fully melts into magma. Later, this magma cools and hardens into a new solid rock. The rock started as metamorphic but is now a different type. Explain what type of rock it is now and why the rock cycle changed it into that type instead of back into metamorphic rock.
choices: It is metamorphic rock again, because heat and pressure underground always transform rock back into the same type it was before
It is igneous rock, because full melting followed by cooling defines how igneous rock forms, not metamorphic rock
It is sedimentary rock, because melting represents an extreme weathering process that breaks the rock into fragments that later harden
It is sedimentary rock, because any rock that has been underground must cool and compress into sedimentary layers before forming new rock
hints: The key difference is whether the rock fully melted or was just squeezed by heat and pressure. What happened here?
Metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock is changed WITHOUT fully melting. If it fully melts, it becomes a different type.

problemText: Two students disagree about the rock cycle. Student A says, 'A sedimentary rock always becomes a metamorphic rock when it goes deep underground.' Student B says, 'A sedimentary rock might become metamorphic rock, or it might become igneous rock instead, depending on what happens to it underground.' Which student is correct, and what determines which type the sedimentary rock becomes?
choices: Student A is correct, because going deep underground always applies enough pressure to cause metamorphic change in any rock type
Student A is correct, because metamorphic rock is the middle stage that all rocks must pass through in the rock cycle
Student B is correct, because whether the rock fully melts or only gets squeezed by heat and pressure decides what it becomes
Student B is correct, because sedimentary rock left underground begins to dissolve and reform into different minerals that create igneous texture
hints: The lesson says the rock cycle has no single path every rock must follow. What decides what happens to a rock?
Think about the difference between a rock that fully melts versus a rock that is squeezed by heat and pressure — which process leads to which type?

problemText: A sedimentary rock is buried so deep underground that intense heat and pressure squeeze and change it, but it never fully melts. Years later, the rock is pushed back to the surface by geological forces. At the surface, this rock breaks into small loose pieces. These loose pieces settle into layers at the bottom of a new ocean, get pressed and glued together over millions of years, and form a new solid rock. Trace this journey through the rock cycle: Name the types of rock at each stage (after the first squeeze, and after the new pressing), and explain why the rock became each type.
choices: First metamorphic (squeezed without melting), then igneous (broken and pressed into new layers)
First igneous (extreme pressure causes partial melting), then sedimentary (pressed and cooled at the surface)
First sedimentary (broken into loose pieces at the surface), then metamorphic (pressed deep underground again)
First metamorphic (squeezed without melting), then sedimentary (loose pieces pressed together into new layers)
hints: After the first stage of squeezing without melting, what is the rock called? Then, after loose pieces are pressed together, what is the second type?
When loose pieces of rock settle and are pressed together, that is always sedimentary rock, no matter what the loose pieces came from.

problemText: A solid rock sits on a mountainside. Over many years, freezing water inside tiny cracks slowly breaks the rock into smaller pieces. These pieces stay in the exact same spot where the rock originally sat. What is this process called?
choices: Sediment formation
Erosion
Deposition
Weathering
hints: Look for the key phrase: does the material break apart, or does it move to a new location?
The lesson says weathering breaks material apart 'right where it already sits.'

problemText: A loose piece of sand is sitting on a desert floor. A strong wind picks it up and carries it rolling across the sand for several hundred meters. At the moment the description ends, the wind is still blowing and the sand is still rolling and has not stopped moving. Which process is happening right now?
choices: Erosion, because the wind is carrying an already-loose piece from one place toward another
Weathering, because the wind is breaking down the solid rock structure into smaller separate grains through physical force
Deposition, because the wind has moved the sand to a new location where it will remain permanently settled
Sediment, because the sand grains are now loose particles that can be transported by moving wind and water
hints: The sand was already loose before the wind picked it up, so weathering did not break it apart.
Deposition only happens when a carried piece comes to rest and stops moving. Is the sand still moving?

problemText: A river flows over smooth stones on the streambed. After heavy rain, the fast-moving water carries loose gravel and silt downstream. The current keeps the sediment tumbling and floating along, moving it farther from where it started. The description ends while the sediment is still suspended in the moving water. What name best fits what is happening to the sediment?
choices: Weathering is breaking the gravel into finer pieces as the fast water tumbles them along the riverbed
Erosion is carrying the already-loose sediment away from where it was
Deposition is laying the sediment down on the streambed where it comes to rest and stops moving
Sediment is being created by the moving water as it physically breaks apart the solid rock material
hints: The gravel and silt were already loose — nothing is breaking apart right now.
For deposition to happen, the carrying force must slow down or stop. Is the river still flowing fast?

problemText: A coastal cliff made of soft sandstone has a deep crack running down it. Waves crash at the base of the cliff, and salty spray mists the crack every day. Over months, the salt and sun-drying cause the edges of the crack to crumble slightly, making it wider, always in that same spot on the cliff face. Later, a big storm sends a huge wave up the cliff that smashes into the loosened chunks and washes them out to sea, where they tumble along the ocean floor for miles before getting stuck in a sandy bay. How many of the three processes—weathering, erosion, and deposition—are shown in this story, and in what order do they happen?
choices: Only weathering, because salt and sun-drying are breaking down the crack in the sandstone over months
Weathering and then erosion, because the salt and sun widen the crack in place and then the wave carries loose chunks away
Weathering, erosion, and deposition, because the chunks break free, get carried across the ocean, and finally stop in the sandy bay
Erosion and deposition only, because the wave is the only force that moves material from place to place
hints: Track what happens step-by-step: first the crack widens in place, then the wave carries chunks away, then chunks come to rest somewhere new. Which process matches each step?
Remember that deposition happens when a carried piece 'comes to rest in a new place.' The chunks end up in a sandy bay far from where they broke free.

problemText: A sidewalk has a small bump where the concrete is starting to crack. Rain seeps into the crack and freezes during a cold night, pushing the crack slightly wider. The next day, it thaws. This freeze-thaw cycle repeats many times. Meanwhile, loose dust and tiny concrete chips sit right in and around the crack—they never blow away or wash off anywhere. Now imagine that at some point, a street-cleaning truck comes by and its spray washes a pile of those loose concrete chips into the storm drain, carrying them away downhill. Which statement correctly describes when and why deposition has NOT yet occurred in this scenario?
choices: Deposition has not occurred because the chunks have broken free from the sidewalk, which means they are only being weathered
Deposition has not occurred because concrete cannot be deposited in a storm drain, only natural rock can be
Deposition has not occurred because the freeze-thaw cycle only weathers the concrete without moving it, and the carried chunks are still traveling toward the storm drain
Deposition has not occurred because the carrying water has not yet slowed down or stopped, so the chunks are being eroded but have not come to rest anywhere
hints: Deposition requires two things: a piece that was already carried AND that piece must now come to rest. Is the water still moving the chunks, or have they stopped?
The test for deposition is: has a carried piece come to rest in a new spot? If it is still being washed along, it is still being eroded.

problemText: A student reads the following description and makes a claim: 'Wind blows across a rocky hilltop. It picks up tiny grains of rock dust that were already loose on the surface. The wind carries the dust downwind for a long distance. When the wind hits a dense forest on the far side of a valley, the trees slow the wind dramatically. The dust falls out of the air and lands on the ground and leaves at the forest edge.' The student says, 'This shows weathering, because the wind is breaking the rock into dust.' Identify what is wrong with the student's reasoning, and state which process or processes the description actually shows.
choices: The student is wrong because the rock dust was already loose before the wind arrived, so nothing was broken apart by the wind. The description shows only erosion and deposition, not weathering.

The student is wrong because weathering requires chemical breakdown or freezing cycles, not just the physical movement of wind carrying particles. The description shows erosion as the wind picks up loose dust and deposition as it settles in the forest.

The student is wrong because the dust actually does deposit in the forest when the wind slows down, and the original rock was already weathered before the wind arrived. The description shows erosion and deposition happening in sequence.

The student is wrong because rock dust that is already loose on the surface means weathering happened in the past, not during the wind event itself. The description shows erosion carrying the dust and deposition when it falls in the forest.
hints: The description says the dust was 'already loose on the surface' before the wind picked it up. If it was already loose, did the wind break it apart?

Weathering breaks solid material apart in one place. Erosion carries already-loose material to a new place. Deposition drops carried material when the carrying force slows. Which two of these three match this story?
